o:
We must simulate `volume` individual droplets falling at index `k`. Each droplet rests on top of the current level at its column, where level = terrain height + water already there. It moves left if some column to the left has a strictly lower level reachable by never going above the starting level; otherwise it tries right; otherwise it stays. Because levels change after every drop, we simply re-evaluate from scratch for each droplet.

**Example 1** (`heights = [2,1,1,2,1,2,2]`, k=3): Drop 1: left scan finds level 1 at index 2 < 2, so it settles at index 2 → `[2,1,2,2,1,2,2]`. Drop 2: left again finds index 1 (level 1) → `[2,2,2,2,1,2,2]`. Drop 3: left is now blocked (all levels ≥ 2), right finds index 4 (level 1) → `[2,2,2,2,2,2,2]`. Drop 4: neither side offers a fall below level 2, so it stacks at k=3 → `[2,2,2,3,2,2,2]`.

**Example 3** (`[3,1,3]`, volume=5, k=1): drops fill the valley symmetrically — left preference fills index 0 first, then right, alternating until all columns reach level 4.

Constraints are tiny (n ≤ 100, volume ≤ 2000), so an O(volume · n) simulation (~200k operations) is more than fast enough.
k: Simulate each droplet independently: try moving left to the lowest reachable level, then right, else stay at k.
A droplet can only move through columns whose level is ≤ its starting level; among valid positions it picks the lowest level, tie-broken by the farthest index in that direction.
With n ≤ 100 and volume ≤ 2000, O(volume · n) brute force is perfectly acceptable.

a.i: For each of the `volume` droplets, scan left from k while the next level is not higher than the current best level, remembering the last position that was strictly lower than heights[k]. If such a position exists, add water there; otherwise do the same scan to the right; otherwise add water at k. This exactly mirrors the rules: prefer left, then right, then stay. Correctness follows because any move sequence must be non-increasing in level until the final fall, so the farthest lowest point reachable without climbing is where the droplet lands.
s: Maintain the mutable array `heights` representing terrain + water.
For each droplet: set best = k, cur = heights[k]; walk i = k-1 down to 0; if heights[i] > cur break, else if heights[i] < cur set best = i, cur = heights[i].
If best != k, increment heights[best] and continue to the next droplet.
Otherwise repeat the same scan to the right (i = k+1 .. n-1); if a lower spot exists, increment heights[best].
If neither side works, increment heights[k]. Return heights after all droplets.
a.t: O(volume · n) — each of up to 2000 droplets triggers two linear scans over at most 100 columns.
a.sp: O(1) extra space — we mutate the input array in place.

a.n: Approach 2: Full-Range Scan Without Early Break (Cleaner Invariant)
a.i: Instead of breaking on the first rise, scan the entire left side and pick the position minimizing (level, distance-from-k) lexicographically — but only among positions whose level never exceeds heights[k] along the path. Since the terrain between k and any candidate must stay ≤ heights[k] for the droplet to travel there, we can just track a running minimum: scan all the way left keeping the last index achieving the strict minimum level seen so far, provided no prefix exceeded heights[k]. Scanning fully avoids subtle off-by-one issues with early termination and makes the 'farthest lowest point' rule explicit. Complexity is unchanged but the logic is easier to verify.
s: For each droplet, define a helper that scans direction d ∈ {-1, +1} from k.
Track `cur` = minimum level seen so far and `best` = last index attaining it; stop following updates if heights[i] exceeds heights[k] (droplet cannot climb past its start).
Prefer the left helper's result if it found a level strictly below heights[k]; otherwise use the right helper's result.
If neither found a lower level, place the droplet at k.
Increment the chosen cell and repeat for all `volume` droplets.
a.t: O(volume · n) — same asymptotic cost as Approach 1; each droplet does two full directional scans.
a.sp: O(1) extra space — in-place updates only.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1: it directly encodes the problem rules and interviewers expect the simulation. Mention Approach 2 as a refactor that centralizes the directional scan into a helper, reducing duplicated code and edge-case bugs. **Pitfalls:** (1) forgetting that the droplet may only pass through cells with level ≤ its *starting* level — comparing against the running minimum instead of heights[k] breaks Example 1; (2) tie-breaking: when several cells share the minimal level, the droplet travels to the *last* (farthest) one, which the 'update on strict improvement' pattern handles naturally; (3) updating heights[k] even when it doesn't move (stacking water). **Edge cases:** volume = 0 (return input unchanged), flat terrain (everything piles at k), valley at the array boundary, and k = 0 or n-1. **Follow-ups:** handle large volume efficiently (e.g., detect periodic fill patterns or use a priority queue over basin cells for O((n + volume log n)) behavior), or generalize to multiple pour points / 2D terrain.
